title: the Markandeya
tomorrow: a book read aloud in a house where someone has died. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Markandeya, and Madalasa's lullaby: the name was only made up for you. Her older sons heard it and left for the forest. Her youngest was raised for the throne, with one gift for later.

Some people keep a note on their phone for bad days: a kind text, screenshotted, a list of reasons to keep going. In the Markandeya Purana, Madalasa gives her youngest son, Alarka, the old version. A ring, with a message tucked inside, and one instruction: open this only when things are very bad. He rules, and the years go by. Then his own brother Subahu marches on him with an allied king's army, and Alarka is losing.
screen: `A NOTE FOR BAD DAYS.` → `A RING FROM HIS MOTHER.` → `OPEN ONLY ON THE WORST DAY.`

segments.voice: The question underneath: what do you do when you can't let go? Alarka opens the ring. In paraphrase it says: give up attachment; if you can't, keep company with the good, because good company is the cure for it. So he goes looking for good company and finds the sage Dattatreya, who doesn't hand him a battle plan. He asks who, really, is suffering here, and teaches what the lullaby once taught his brothers: the self isn't the body, or the kingdom, or the losing of it. Then the twist. Subahu, as the story tells it, never wanted the kingdom; he came only to bring Alarka to this. A neighbor tradition says something close. In a Buddhist sutta, the Buddha's attendant Ananda suggests that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answers: not half. The whole of it. What the two share: good company isn't a nice extra on the way; it's the way. An honest difference: Dattatreya points Alarka toward a self that was never the body or the kingdom. The Buddha's teaching speaks of no such lasting self. They agree about the friend, and differ about what the friend helps you see.
screen: `WHEN YOU CAN'T LET GO?` · `THE RING: KEEP GOOD COMPANY.` · `ANANDA: HALF? THE BUDDHA: ALL.` · `ONE FRIEND, TWO VIEWS OF SELF.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY IS THE CURE.`

segments.voice: Count, on your fingers, the people who leave you steadier after you've been with them. One finger for each person, and one slow breath for each. If you run out of fingers, keep counting on the breath.
The Markandeya. A Purana where one teaching reaches Madalasa's sons twice: in the cradle, and through a ring on a hard day.
Your line: the Markandeya. If you can't let go, keep good company, the ring says. Rest well.

howItsDone: Hindus speak of satsang, the company of the good, as a support on the spiritual path, often meaning gatherings to sing and hear teaching together; Buddhists speak of kalyanamitta, the admirable friend.

fork.setup: a friend reads Alarka's ring next to the Buddha's words to Ananda and asks how they fit together. what's the fairest answer?
options: same teaching; every religion says exactly this.
both put good company at the center; they differ on what it helps you see.
nothing in common; one is Hindu and one is Buddhist.
fork.reveal: the ring calls good company the cure for clinging; the Buddha calls it the whole of the path. Dattatreya teaches a self beyond the body; the Buddha teaches no lasting self.

original.note: Sanskrit: sat-sanga, company with the good, what the ring offers when letting go is too hard.

what a scholar hears: the ring's verse makes sanga, attachment, the problem and sat-sanga, good company, the cure; Dattatreya then teaches Alarka the self.

chat.meaning: Madalasa's ring: give up attachment; if you can't, keep company with the good, because good company is the cure.

Alarka.meaning: Madalasa's youngest son, raised to be king

Subahu.meaning: Alarka's older brother, who left for the forest

Dattatreya.meaning: a revered sage and teacher who instructs Alarka

notes: 2026-10-14 recipe v3 rewrite (wisdom shape, unity thread): kept title, word, carry, the Markandeya source and the story of the 2026-10-13 draft; added the Buddhist neighbor. Shared: good company is the path, not an extra. Honest difference: Dattatreya teaches a self beyond body and kingdom; the Buddha's teaching (anatta) speaks of no lasting self. A Buddhist reader and a Hindu Keeper should confirm both sides are fair and neither is ranked.
SN 45.2 paraphrased (no quotation): Ananda says admirable friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha says not so, it is the whole. Confirm the paraphrase.
The ring's verse (sangah sarvatmana tyajyah ... sa sadbhih saha kartavyah, santah sangasya bheshajam) is paraphrased; confirm wording and chapter.
Subahu's motive ('he came only to bring Alarka to this') follows the Markandeya Purana's telling; confirm.
Original सत्सङ्ग: the word isn't in the ring's verse as one compound; the note calls it what the ring offers. Confirm or swap.
Priya: her best friend Sam pulls her back out to the last garba nights (follows 1515's double-booking, resolved by talking to both). Practice kind: a gratitude count.
